All I'm saying is that the "traditional" use of a `.env` file is to store secrets that are specific to the particular installation, and that in this usage model the `.env` file should obviously not be committed to source control. This example goes against this traditional usage, by creating an incentive for users to commit the file.

Flask config files are different in my opinion. Those can have non-sensitive values. Sensitive values in config files should import from the environment (such as from the `.env` file that should not be on source control).

discussion_comments.comment_body:
Let me summarize. It will be very tempting to use the `.env` just so that you don't have to think about `FLASK_APP` anymore. As such, one might be inclined to commit this `.env` file to git, so that you don't have to make one in every machine the app is installed. Since many other frameworks use a `.env` file as a place to store secrets, this presents a conflict, in my opinion. We would be using the .env file in a different way that what I consider the norm.

As another issue, having ` .env` file that is not imported when you run the app in production via gunicorn, etc. is also a problem, if you use it to store other settings that are needed by the application, besides `FLASK_APP` and `FLASK_DEBUG`.

For `FLASK_APP`, I would rather implement some sort of default, so that you don't have to rely on configuration. For example, I would be okay with `FLASK_APP` defaulting to `wsgi:application`. You then write a two line `wsgi.py`, safely commit it to git and be done with it.
